passage:
Vandana, you say you will never forgive the friend who told your secret. Let me tell you mine. I'm Harsha. At sixteen my best friend Naveen told the whole class my father had lost his job. For five years I replayed it. I told myself forgiving would mean it hadn't mattered, and it had mattered.
In my twenties my aunt said, "You're carrying his mistake in your bag, and he isn't even here." I realised forgiving didn't mean being friends again or saying it was fine. It meant I could put the weight down. I did, for me. I never went back to that friendship. Naveen wrote once, and I didn't reply, and that was fine.
But my shoulders felt different after.

qa.q: What did Naveen tell the class?
qa.a: Naveen told the whole class that Harsha's father had lost his job.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling during the five years of replaying it?
qa.a: Harsha felt angry and hurt, holding the grudge because forgiving seemed to mean the harm hadn't mattered.

qa.q: What choice inside the story eased the weight without reopening the friendship?
qa.a: Harsha chose to put the weight down for Harsha's own sake, without going back to the friendship or saying it was fine.

qa.q: What did the aunt see when she said Harsha was carrying Naveen's mistake in a bag?
qa.a: The aunt saw that the grudge was costing Harsha while Naveen was not even there to feel it. She named it in a picture, not a lecture.

grounding: An elder recalls holding a grudge because forgiving seemed to mean the harm did not matter; letting go was a release without reconciliation.

passage:
The science-fair project was due at nine the next morning, and Rashmi's only partner was Chinmay, the boy who had told the class about her diary last term. Every time he spoke on the group call she felt the old heat rise in her face. Forgiving him would mean it hadn't mattered, she thought, and it had mattered a lot. The wifi kept dropping.
At eleven at night he sent, "I'm sorry about the diary. I know it was a rotten thing."
She stared at it. Then she wrote, "It was. I'm not ready to be friends. Send me slide four."
"Okay," he wrote.
She felt strange: still angry, but the grip had loosened by one finger. They finished at midnight.

qa.q: What was due at nine the next morning?
qa.a: The science-fair project was due at nine.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling whenever Chinmay spoke on the call?
qa.a: Rashmi felt hot with old anger and hurt, since forgiving him seemed to mean the harm had not mattered.

qa.q: What choice did Rashmi make at eleven that let the project move forward?
qa.a: Rashmi answered that it was a rotten thing, said she was not ready to be friends and asked for slide four. She worked with him without pretending it was fine.

qa.q: What might Chinmay have been feeling when he sent the apology?
qa.a: Chinmay was probably guilty and nervous, hoping for a reply. Sending the apology so late suggests he had been working up to it.

grounding: A teenager replays an old betrayal and refuses to forgive, feeling forgiveness would mean the harm did not matter; letting go does not require friendship.

passage: Baljeet was sixteen and still couldn't look at Abhinav in the school corridor. A year ago, Baljeet had told him about his parents' fights, and within a week half the class knew. Abhinav had apologised twice. Baljeet had refused both times. Every time he saw Abhinav, the whole week replayed: the whispers, the looks, his face burning. "If I forgive him, it's like saying it didn't matter," he told his elder cousin Harleen one evening in the Dehradun flat. Harleen shook her head. "Forgiving doesn't mean it didn't matter. It means you stop carrying it around every day. You don't have to be friends again." Baljeet was quiet for a long time. The next day, when Abhinav passed, Baljeet nodded once. Not friendly. Just done. Walking home, he noticed he hadn't replayed that week at all.

qa.q: How many times had Abhinav apologised?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he saw Abhinav in the corridor?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry, as the whole week of whispers and his burning face replayed every time.

qa.q: How did Harleen help Baljeet think about forgiveness differently?
qa.a: She explained that forgiving doesn't mean the harm didn't matter; it means he stops carrying it, and he doesn't have to be friends again.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt when Baljeet nodded once?
qa.a: Abhinav may have felt a small relief and a sense of closure, even though they aren't friends again.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying a betrayal and refusing to forgive, and learning that letting go is a release for himself, not approval.

passage:
"Anand, you're still angry about the science fair?"
"He stole my idea, Santosh bhaiya. The solar cooker. He won with it."
"That was eight months ago."
"So? I still think about it every day."
"And you want him to say sorry?"
"He did. Twice. I don't care."
Santosh bhaiya sat down on the bed. "What do you think forgiving him would mean?"
"That what he did was fine."
"No. It'd mean you stop letting him live in your head. You don't have to trust him. You don't have to be friends."
Anand was quiet. "So I'd forgive for me, not for him?"
"Exactly. For you."
Anand looked out the window. "I'm tired of being angry."
"Then maybe put it down."

qa.q: What was Anand's science fair idea?
qa.a: The solar cooker.

qa.q: How did Anand seem to feel by the end of the talk?
qa.a: Anand felt tired of being angry and ready to consider letting go.

qa.q: What would you advise Anand now?
qa.a: Anand could decide to stop replaying it, maybe by writing it down once and choosing to let it rest, without needing to be friends again.

qa.q: How does Santosh bhaiya see forgiveness?
qa.a: He sees it as a release for Anand, not approval of what happened or a need to trust the other boy.

grounding: Shows a teenager holding a grudge who learns that letting go is a release for oneself and does not mean approving the act.

passage:
In Class 9, Rehana told everyone I cheated in the maths test. I didn't. The teacher believed me after a week, but by then everyone had heard.
For a whole year I replayed it. In the shower, on the bus, before sleep. I rehearsed speeches I'd never give. When Rehana said sorry at the Class 10 farewell, I walked away. I thought if I forgave her, it would mean the lie was okay.
Then one night I realised I'd spent more time thinking about Rehana than about my own friends. She had moved on. I was still stuck.
So I decided to forgive, not for her, but for me. I didn't message her. I didn't become her friend. I just stopped rehearsing speeches.
I'm Aadhya. Rehana still isn't my friend, and that's fine. But I sleep better.

qa.q: What did Rehana tell everyone?
qa.a: That the narrator cheated in the maths test.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling during the year of replaying?
qa.a: Aadhya felt angry and stuck, rehearsing speeches and believing forgiving would make the lie okay.

qa.q: What did Aadhya's way of forgiving get right?
qa.a: It released Aadhya from replaying the harm without needing to reconcile or approve of what Rehana did.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt when Aadhya walked away at the farewell?
qa.a: Rehana was probably hurt or embarrassed, having tried to apologise.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying an old betrayal and learning that forgiving is a release for oneself, not reconciliation or approval.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Wednesday.
Ramesh came in because his class teacher noticed he walks out whenever Indu enters the room. Last year Indu forwarded a screenshot of his private message to the class group. He still replays it, he says, "every time I see her face." When I asked what forgiving would mean to him, he said, "That it was fine. It wasn't fine." I told him that letting go is for his own peace; it does not mean saying it was okay, and he does not have to be friends with her again. He was quiet, then asked, "So I can still think it was wrong?" Yes. He agreed to try writing the whole story down once, then deciding what he still wants to carry. Next session Friday.

qa.q: What did Indu do last year?
qa.a: Indu forwarded a screenshot of Ramesh's private message to the class group.

qa.q: What does Ramesh fear forgiving would mean?
qa.a: He fears it would mean saying the betrayal was fine, and he still feels hurt and angry because it wasn't.

qa.q: What small step did Ramesh agree to try?
qa.a: Writing the whole story down once and then deciding what he still wants to carry.

qa.q: How might Indu feel each time Ramesh walks out of the room?
qa.a: Indu may feel guilty or awkward, and the walking out keeps the old betrayal alive for both of them.

grounding: Shows a teenager holding a grudge because forgiving feels like approving the betrayal, and a counsellor separating release from reconciliation.
